headline: Nvidia's boss steps down after reports about a spy

sources.title: NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition (Nvidia statement, SEC filing)
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after affair with suspected Chinese spy (NBC News)
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid spy scandal and market loss (Al Jazeera)
Nvidia launches investigation into CEO's alleged relationship with Chinese spy (NPR)
The spying affair scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could shape the US-China AI race (ABC News)

chunks.text: Jensen Huang {{stepped down}} as the head of Nvidia on November 12, 2026. Nvidia is an American company that makes computer [[chips]], tiny parts that work like a computer's brain. Its chips run many [[artificial intelligence]], or AI, systems. Huang, 63, helped {{set up}} the company 33 years ago. He left his job as [[chief executive]] right away. He also left the [[board of directors]], which oversees the company. Nvidia did not give a reason. Huang left after reports about his [[private life]], including a relationship with a woman U.S. officials [[suspect]] is a Chinese spy.

verbs.why: A leader often steps down after a big mistake. Some coaches step down when the team loses too often. Jensen Huang stepped down as the head of Nvidia on November 12, 2026.

verbs.wrong: To work for a big business
verbs.why: Many young people set up their own businesses online. Two friends often set up a company together after college. Huang helped set up Nvidia 33 years ago.

chunks.text: The spy claims first {{came out}} in The New York Times on October 29. It said U.S. [[intelligence agencies]], the government's spy services, believe a Chinese businesswoman worked for China's spy agency. A company in Singapore that she once led bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips. The U.S. bans sales of Nvidia's best chips to China for security reasons. Reports say she may have helped China {{get around}} those [[limits]]. China {{hit back}} and called the claims [[smears]], false stories meant to hurt China.

verbs.correct: To become known to the public
verbs.wrong: To be sold for a high price
verbs.why: The truth usually comes out in the end. New facts come out when reporters ask more questions. The spy claims first came out in The New York Times on October 29.

verbs.correct: To find a way to avoid a rule
verbs.wrong: To ask for a change to a rule
verbs.why: Some students get around the phone rule by hiding their phones in their bags. People sometimes get around a ticket limit by using a friend's name. The reports say the businesswoman may have helped China get around American limits on chip sales.

verbs.correct: To answer an attack with strong words
verbs.wrong: To ask for more time to answer
verbs.why: Politicians often hit back when someone attacks them. The singer hits back at bad reviews online. China hit back and called the spy claims smears against China.

chunks.text: On November 8, Huang {{owned up to}} the relationship in an email to workers. He [[apologized]] to his wife. The same day, Nvidia's board said it would {{look into}} the reports. It {{brought in}} [[outside lawyers]] to help. Federal police and Congress are also investigating. Some [[shareholders]], who own part of the company, [[sued]] Nvidia.

verbs.correct: To admit that you did something wrong
verbs.wrong: To promise to work much harder
verbs.why: Good players own up to their mistakes. A child often owns up to a broken window when a parent asks. In an email to Nvidia workers, Huang owned up to the relationship with the woman.

verbs.wrong: To print a story in the paper
verbs.why: The police look into every report of a stolen car. A good school looks into a problem when a parent calls. On November 8, 2026, Nvidia's board said it would look into the reports about its boss.

verbs.correct: To get outside experts to help
verbs.wrong: To send workers to a new office
verbs.why: Schools bring in experts when a problem is serious. Many companies bring in lawyers when there is a legal problem. Nvidia's board brought in outside lawyers to help with its investigation.

chunks.text: Nvidia's [[stock price]] {{went down}} more than 11% after the news. The company's finance chief will {{take over}} as chief executive for now. The board will search for a [[permanent]] boss. Nvidia also named the first chair, or leader, of its board. It will still report its [[earnings]] on November 17. [[Lawmakers]] in Congress want to {{find out}} whether U.S. secrets were at risk.

verbs.wrong: To be sold to a new owner
verbs.why: Gas prices often go down in the fall. The price of a new phone goes down after a year. Nvidia's stock price went down more than 11% after the news on November 12.

verbs.correct: To start doing someone else's job
verbs.why: A new manager often takes over when the old one leaves. The vice president takes over when the president is sick. Nvidia's finance chief will take over as chief executive for now.

verbs.correct: To learn facts that were not known
verbs.wrong: To share news with the public
verbs.why: Doctors run tests to find out what is wrong. Students find out their grades at the end of the week. Lawmakers in Congress want to find out whether American secrets were at risk.

mainIdea.s: Nvidia's boss, Jensen Huang, has quit after reports linked him to a woman suspected of spying for China. China denies the claims, and the finance chief now runs the firm.
mainIdea.why: Huang stepped down right away, after the spy claims came out. China hit back, and Nvidia's finance chief will take over for now.

mainIdea.s: Jensen Huang has left his top job at Nvidia because U.S. officials charged him with spying. He will remain on the board, and Nvidia has explained the reason in detail.
mainIdea.why: Close, but officials suspect the woman, not Huang, of spying. Huang also left the board, and Nvidia did not give a reason.

mainIdea.s: A large American chip company plans to build a new factory to make AI chips at home. Leaders say the plant will create thousands of jobs and help the country compete with China.
mainIdea.why: This is about Nvidia's boss, who stepped down after reports about a suspected Chinese spy. The company's finance chief will take over for now.

lines.text: Did you hear? Jensen Huang {{stepped down}} as the head of Nvidia.
What? Wow, I [[didn't see that coming]]. He helped {{set up}} that company.
I know. He left right away, and the company didn't say why.
Is this about that spy story?
Probably. It first {{came out}} in October. U.S. officials think a woman he had a relationship with was a Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang, [[of all people]]? What did he say?
He {{owned up to}} the relationship and said sorry to his wife.
And the board decided to {{look into}} it?
Yes. They {{brought in}} outside lawyers, and Congress is asking questions too.
So he's been [[under fire]] for a while.
Right. And China {{hit back}}. It says the spy claims are false.
Well, nothing has been proven. People are [[innocent until proven guilty]].
True. But the stock still {{went down}} more than 11%.
Wow. So who's running the company now?
The finance chief will {{take over}} for now. She's been there since 2013, so she's [[a steady hand]].
Good. I bet lawmakers still want to {{find out}} if any secrets were at risk.
Definitely. This story isn't finished yet.

expressions.def: Used when something happens that you did not expect at all
ex: She quit her job to become a chef? I didn't see that coming.

expressions.def: Used to show surprise that a certain person is part of something
ex: My dad, of all people, joined a dance class.

expressions.def: Used to say no one should be treated as guilty before a court decides
ex: The police arrested him, but he is innocent until proven guilty.
Remember, people are innocent until proven guilty.

expressions.def: A calm person you can trust to lead in a hard time
ex: The school needs a steady hand after a difficult year.
Our new manager is a steady hand when things go wrong.
